lesson.title: What r Does and Does Not Care About
lesson.summary: Correlation is unitless, symmetric in its two variables, bounded between negative 1 and 1, and unaffected by rescaling, which makes it portable but also easy to over trust.
lesson.body:
Once a correlation coefficient is computed, it is worth knowing exactly what kind of number it is, because r behaves in ways that surprise students who first meet it. Four properties, in particular, explain both its usefulness for summarizing a relationship and its limits, which the next chapter takes up directly. First, r is always between negative 1 and positive 1, inclusive, no matter what the original variables measure or how large the data set is. A value of exactly 1 means the points fall on a perfectly rising straight line, exactly negative 1 means a perfectly falling straight line, and 0 means no linear association at all. Everything else falls somewhere between those anchors, and the closer r sits to either negative 1 or 1, the more tightly the points cluster around a straight line. The hours studied example from the previous chapter, with r about 0.99, sits almost at the strong positive end of that scale, just short of a perfect line.

Second, r has no units, even though the original variables do. Hours studied is measured in hours and exam score in points, but r is just a pure number, about 0.99, with nothing attached. This follows directly from how it is built: every term in the calculation is a product of z-scores, and a z-score itself has no units, because it is a difference divided by a standard deviation measured in the same original units, which cancels out completely in the division.

Third, r treats the two variables symmetrically. Swapping which variable is called x and which is called y and recomputing gives back exactly the same r, because multiplying zx by zy gives the same result as multiplying zy by zx. Correlation alone never tells you which variable is doing the explaining and which is responding, that distinction has to come from the context of the study and how the data were collected, not from the arithmetic of r itself.

Fourth, r is unaffected by changing the units of either variable, as long as the change is a linear rescaling, such as converting hours to minutes or feet to meters. Multiplying every x-value by 60 to convert hours into minutes changes the mean and standard deviation of x by that same factor of 60, so every z-score comes out identical to before, and r stays at 0.99. This is a real strength of correlation: it describes the shape of the relationship itself, not the scale someone happened to choose for measuring it.

These properties combine to make r especially useful for comparison. Because r has no units and always stays within a fixed range of negative 1 to 1, it is possible to directly compare the strength of two completely different relationships, say, the relationship between hours studied and exam score against the relationship between a person's height and weight, even though one pair of variables is measured in hours and points and the other in inches and pounds. A raw slope could never be compared this way, since points per hour and pounds per inch are not even the same kind of quantity, but two correlation coefficients, both pure numbers between negative 1 and 1, sit on equal footing and can be ranked directly. Together these four properties make r a clean, portable summary of linear strength, but clean is not the same as complete, and the next chapter turns to exactly where a strong r can still mislead.
